newsitem.title: USA: Fund investors staying in U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: Fund investors staying in U.S. stocks.

text.p: Mutual fund investors are still plowing cash into U.S. stocks despite the plunge in the market but are also seeking shelter from the volatility in money market and international funds, analysts said.
"The inclination to hold is really deeply ingrained since it's paid off," said John Rekenthaler, publisher of Morningstar Mutual Funds. "Habits are hard to break, and right now the habit is to hold."
However, Bob Adler, president of AMG Data Services, said slowing cash flows into growth and income and index funds indicate that investor sentiment may be turning negative towards large-cap stocks.
"Despite the fact the sector continues to take in money, the four week moving average....continues to decline," he said. "That may have been one of the factors triggering the selloff in that area."
The Dow Jones industrial average continued to unravel from its record close of 7,085.16 set on March 11, spooked by fears of rising interest rates and weaker earnings.
The index lost 134 points last week, including a 148-point tumble on Friday, to close at 6,392.
Investors put about $4.1 billion into stock funds, including $2.2 billion into growth funds, for the week ended April 9, Adler said.

However, new investments into international funds totalled about $700 million for the week, up from around $300 million the previous two weeks, he said. Corporate bond funds have also turned more popular, he said. "There appears to be some reallocation both to international funds and investment grade corporate bond funds," Adler said.

Vanguard Group said flows into its index funds have slowed recently but remain positive. "So far it seems that Vanguard investors are unfazed by the market activity," said Vanguard spokesman John Worth. "We are receiving more calls on IRA contributions and tax-related questions than the market."
Charles Biderman, editor of Liquidity Trim Tabs, said flows into money market funds have increased in the last two weeks, but by-and-large, investors are staying in stocks.
"Investors are still standing pat and they're not bailing out yet," he said. "It is surprising that they are as confident as they have been."
After the April 15 tax deadline, one incentive to buy money market funds or growth funds for IRAs will be gone and sentiment may shift, he said.
"Maybe next week we'll have a better idea of what the sentiment is post tax-time," he said.
